title: Query complexity of envy-free cake cutting
short_statement: Determine the deterministic worst-case query complexity of complete exact envy-free cake cutting; newer randomized expected bounds are a distinct result.
open_problem: Give a substantially better upper bound, a superquadratic lower bound, or the true asymptotic query complexity for exact envy-free cake cutting.
background: Cake cutting is a canonical fair-division model for divisible heterogeneous resources. Existence of envy-free allocations is classical, but algorithmic access to valuations matters: protocols cannot inspect arbitrary value measures directly. The Robertson-Webb model formalizes access through cut and evaluation queries. For decades, a major open question asked whether a bounded finite envy-free protocol exists for every number of agents. Aziz and Mackenzie answered yes, with a historical tower-of-exponentials query bound, subsequently improved as recorded below. The resulting problem is not whether envy-free cake cutting is possible; it is to understand the true information complexity of finding such allocations under the standard query model.
full_statement: A cake is the interval $[0,1]$. Each of $n$ agents has a nonatomic additive valuation measure over subintervals. In the Robertson-Webb model, a protocol may ask evaluation queries $\mathrm{Eval}_i(x,y)$, returning agent $i$'s value for $[x,y]$, and cut queries $\mathrm{Cut}_i(x,\alpha)$, returning a point $y$ such that agent $i$ values $[x,y]$ at $\alpha$ when such a point exists. An allocation, possibly using disconnected pieces, is envy-free if every agent weakly prefers its own allocated piece to every other agent's piece. Let $Q(n)$ be the minimum worst-case number of Robertson-Webb queries required by a bounded deterministic protocol that always terminates and returns a complete exact envy-free allocation for every profile of nonatomic additive valuations. Determine the asymptotic growth of $Q(n)$, or give substantially tighter upper and lower bounds.
known_results: Aziz and Mackenzie established bounded exact protocols, and Procaccia proved a quadratic query lower bound. Ye and Bai, 'Cutting Down the Tower: Single-Exponential Envy-Free Cake Cutting' (arXiv:2609.05191v1), give a deterministic $n^{O(1)}2^n$ upper bound for complete exact envy-freeness with disconnected shares. Mackenzie and Suzuki, 'Exact Envy-Free Cake Cutting with Polynomial Expected Queries' (arXiv:2610.28535v1), Theorem 1, report a Las Vegas protocol with $\widetilde O(n^{30})$ expected Robertson-Webb queries, using independent uniform cake-point samples. It terminates almost surely and never outputs an incorrect allocation. Remark 1.1 extends the hungry-agent presentation to valuations with zero-valued intervals. This does not give a deterministic polynomial worst-case bound.

progress.summary: The deterministic upper bound is single-exponential; a separate randomized expected-polynomial result is reported. The deterministic target is not resolved.

counterexample_rationale: Lower-bound adversaries can be finite query-answer constructions, but proving strong lower bounds requires adversarial valuation families rather than ordinary finite examples.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search may help design smaller protocols or adversary strategies for small $n$, but asymptotic query lower bounds are proof-heavy.

literature.synthesis: Exactness, completeness, disconnected shares, expected query count, and deterministic worst-case count must be kept separate. The old tower is no longer the upper-bound frontier.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Study the updated deterministic protocol and distinguish derandomization from expected-complexity analysis. A worst-case query bound must hold for every valuation profile and execution.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: Protocols must use only Robertson-Webb queries and terminate after a bound depending on $n$ but independent of the particular valuation descriptions. The returned allocation must be exactly envy-free for arbitrary nonatomic additive valuations; approximate envy-freeness, free-disposal partial allocations, connected-piece relaxations, or special valuation classes do not solve this exact problem. A lower bound must be adversarial over valuation measures and query transcripts, not merely over a finite parametric family unless that family is rich enough to support the adversary argument.

where_posed.text: The bounded-protocol breakthrough and enormous upper bound appear in Aziz and Mackenzie, 'A Discrete and Bounded Envy-Free Cake Cutting Protocol for Any Number of Agents'.
